newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: AWU SAYS NEWCASTLE ACTION ABOUT JOB SECURITY

The Australian Workers Union says the industrial campaign over BHP's decision to shut down its Newcastle plant, is not about saving the steelworks, rather maintaining job security. Workers began returning to work last night after a 24 hour strike, the first action in an ongoing industrial campaign, highlighting their concerns for the future of BHP's steelmaking activities. AWU Port Kembla Branch Secretary, Graham Roberts, says unions want to have talks with both BHP and the Federal Government to find a way of reviving the Australian steel industry. The Union says it's set for the biggest industrial campaign against BHP since the early 1980's.

The Trades and Labour Council in Western Australia says international trade sanctions against the state will affect its economy and harm its standing. Unions are predicting the action following the passage of new industrial legislation through State Parliament. They're also predicting that the level of industrial action in the state will increase dramatically in the short term. There'll be further stoppages in the construction, mining, manufacturing and maintenance sectors, as well as further disruption for schools and the public sector. TLC President, Keith Peckham, says its regrettable, but he believes sanctions by unions in the Indian Ocean region and Europe will go ahead.
LONGREACH PM VISIT MAY BE CHANGED

Heavy rain in Longreach may cause the the meeting venue for the Prime Minister's native title meeting on Saturday, to ne moved from the front steps of the Australian Stockmans Hall of Fame. The Hall of Fame's Brian Osborne says while fine weather's forecast for Saturday, the problem of car parking could force the change. n anonuncement on any change of venue will be made by 10 o'clock this morning.
ROBINSON HITS BACK AT PLAN CRITICISM

The Deputy Chair of ATSIC, Ray Robinson, has hit back at criticisms of his native title plan by the Social Justice Commissioner, Mick Dodson. His suggestion, to have family-held pastoral leases converted to freehold, was slammed yesterday by Mr Dodson, who said it didn't represent Aboriginal views. Mr Robinson says conflict between indigenous leaders is nothing new in the Aboriginal community.

A leading airline says the benefits to Australian tourism would be enormous, if Australia was to be granted offical recognition as a tourist destination in China. A formal request will be made this weekend to a Chinese Government tourism official who's currently in Australia. Chairman Her has been meeting with Australian tourism officials, and at the weekend will receive an official request from the Federal Government for China to recognise Australia as an approved destination. If that status is granted, Chinese nationals would be free to travel to Australia for tourism purposes. Tim Acton, from Cathay Pacific, says that would be good news for Australia, with a growing number of people in China described as quite affluent.
DRUGS THE BIGGEST PROBLEM FOR STREET KIDS

A childrens welfare agency says drugs are the biggest problem facing Australia's street kids. Peter Nixon, who works with the Open family Foundation as a street worker, says drugs are becoming too accessible but police are doing all they can to fight the problem. Mr Nixon says with so much money to be made by selling and buying drugs, Police can only do so much. He says street kids are at the end of the rung, and are an easy target for dealers.
